title: Chapter 85 — The Follow-Up System
intro: The sale does not end when the customer pays. Step 10 of the 10 Steps of Selling is Follow-up — and it is where your future income is built. This chapter teaches you how to turn one sale into a lifetime of business.

sections.title: Follow-Up Is Not Optional
sections.content:
Most salespeople spend every morning waiting for the next customer to walk through the door. Elite salespeople spend part of every morning building tomorrow's business.

Follow-up is Step 10 of the 10 Steps of Selling. It is the step most people skip because the commission already hit. But it is the step that separates someone earning $60,000 a year from someone earning $200,000 doing the exact same job on the exact same floor.

Here is the reality: customers replace appliances every several years. They move. They renovate. Their family grows. Friends ask them for recommendations. If they remember you as their appliance expert, you become the first person they contact instead of starting another Google search.

The objective is simple: do not make them remember your company. Make them remember you.

sections.title: The Old-School Advantage
sections.content:
For decades, top-performing salespeople built enormous books of business through small personal touches. Handwritten thank-you cards. Birthday cards. Christmas or holiday cards. Congratulations on a new home. Anniversary of their purchase. Notes after service visits. Simple check-in messages.

The cards were rarely long. Something as simple as: 'Hope you are still loving your new refrigerator. Thank you again for trusting me. If you ever need anything, I am always happy to help.'

That is often enough. Authenticity beats perfection.

In today's transactional society, we have forgotten about the basic necessity of developing relationships with clients. We always wait for the next customer. But having a portfolio makes everything easier — because your next year starts with a warm database, not a cold floor.

sections.title: The Relationship Cadence
sections.content:
Every salesperson should have a follow-up schedule. Not a random one — a deliberate cadence that keeps you connected without being annoying.

Immediately after delivery: thank-you message. Make sure everything arrived correctly.

30 days: satisfaction check. How is the product? Any questions?

6 months: friendly check-in. Quick note. No sales pitch.

12 months: purchase anniversary. Simple reminder that you remember them.

Holiday season: personalized greeting.

Birthdays: simple birthday message.

Warranty milestones: helpful reminders when coverage is approaching expiration.

Every 2 to 3 years: home improvement or renovation check-in. Are they thinking about upgrading anything?

These contacts should never feel like sales pitches. The purpose is to maintain the relationship. Sales happen naturally when trust already exists.

sections.title: Respect Every Customer's Culture
sections.content:
Relationships improve when customers feel understood. Whenever appropriate, acknowledge holidays that are meaningful to them.

Christmas. Hanukkah. Ramadan. Eid. Chinese New Year. Diwali. Easter. Thanksgiving. Other culturally significant celebrations.

This should always be respectful, optional, and based only on information the customer has willingly shared. The goal is thoughtfulness, not assumption. Understanding their culture shows a lot about who you are as a person. Those little touches go a long way.

sections.title: Your CRM Is Your Future Income
sections.content:
Your CRM is not simply a database. It is your future income.

Every satisfied customer becomes another opportunity for repeat sales, additional rooms, rental properties, renovations, vacation homes, family referrals, workplace referrals, and builder or designer introductions.

Over time, your database becomes an asset that compounds in value. The salesperson with the largest network of genuine relationships rarely worries about where the next sale will come from — because they have spent years planting seeds that continue producing long after the original transaction.

Rather than standing around the water cooler gossiping or discussing what happened the day before or blaming bad luck — spend that time managing your CRM. Make sure you are taking care of your own future, your own money, and your own pipeline.

sections.title: Referrals Come From Relationships
sections.content:
Customers who feel remembered are significantly more likely to recommend you, return for future purchases, leave positive reviews, contact you before shopping elsewhere, and introduce friends and family.

Referrals are earned through trust, not requested through pressure. You do not need to ask 'do you know anyone who needs an appliance?' If you stay connected and they have a great experience, the referrals come naturally. When a friend mentions they need a new dishwasher, your customer will say 'go see my person at the store — they took great care of me.'

That referral is worth more than any Google ad. And it cost you nothing except a few minutes of follow-up over the course of a year.

sections.title: The Replacement Cycle Is Your Pipeline
sections.content:
Every appliance has a lifespan. A washer lasts 8 to 12 years. A refrigerator lasts 10 to 15 years. A range lasts 13 to 18 years.

If your CRM tracks what each customer bought and when, you know roughly when they will need a replacement. That is not a guess — it is a prediction based on real data.

Imagine sending a check-in message to a customer seven years after they bought a washer: 'Just wanted to see how your washer is holding up. These models typically start needing more attention around this age. If you are noticing anything, let me know — I am happy to help you explore options before it becomes an emergency.'

That is not a sales pitch. That is genuine service. And it positions you as their go-to person before they even start shopping.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating follow-up, ask:

Does the salesperson have an active CRM with regular customer contact — or is it a dusty database they never open?
Do they follow a deliberate cadence — immediate, 30 days, 6 months, 12 months, holidays?
Do they personalize their outreach or send generic messages?
Do they track what customers bought and when — building a replacement pipeline?
Do they treat follow-up as part of the job or as something extra?
Are referrals coming in naturally from past customers?

Do not think of your customer list as a record of past sales. Think of it as a community of people who trusted you enough to make one of the largest purchases for their home. Protect those relationships.
